headline: Hotter Inflation Puts Rates' Recent Lows at Risk
tileReason: October consumer prices rose faster than forecast this morning, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield up to about 4.93%; the daily 30-year average was 7.18% Monday, near its lowest since September.
takeaway:
Mortgage rates started the day near their lowest since September. The daily 30-year average was 7.18% Monday, up just 0.01% from Friday's 7.17%. Freddie Mac's weekly survey is at 7.18% from last Thursday, and a new reading comes out this Thursday.

This morning's inflation report came in hotter than expected. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus the 0.3% forecasters expected, and core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, the same pace as September. Because last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data, the report has no yearly inflation rate this time.

Bond markets reacted right away. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, jumped to about 4.93% this morning from about 4.88% at Monday's close, and short-term yields rose even more. When yields rise like this during the day, lenders usually raise their rates, so today's daily average is likely to come in higher than Monday's 7.18% when it posts this afternoon.

A Fed official raised the stakes a few hours before the report. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London this morning that he leans toward a quarter-point Fed rate hike in December and that a half-point hike should be considered if core inflation came in around 0.3% or higher, which it did. Futures markets, where traders bet on Fed decisions, now see a December 9 hike as close to certain, with about a 15% chance it is a half point, up from about 1% before the report.

Falling oil is the main thing working in borrowers' favor. Brent crude dropped below $90 a barrel this morning for the first time since August after President Trump said he is holding off on new strikes on Iran following talks with Qatar's prime minister, and U.S. crude is down about 3%. Cheaper oil eases inflation worries, though attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz have not stopped.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.23% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 6, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra-wide gap gives lenders room to absorb part of a bond-market selloff, but not all of one.

The next tests come quickly. The government sells $42 billion of 10-year notes this afternoon, the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, and Thursday brings a 30-year bond sale and Freddie Mac's weekly survey. Friday's wholesale inflation report (PPI) and the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure come next.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.afterLabel: Tue, Nov 10, after Waller's remarks and the hot CPI report
fedOdds.source: The Weekend Spread (Nov 9 close); CME FedWatch via KuCoin/MarsBit and PANews (Nov 10); Yahoo Finance (Nov 10)
fedOdds.note: Sources differ on the starting point: The Weekend Spread put December hike odds near 80% at Monday's close, while CME FedWatch figures reported this morning showed about 99% before the CPI report, after Fed Governor Waller's remarks. After the report, CME FedWatch showed a hike as all but certain: about 85% for a quarter point and about 15% for a half point, up from about 1%. Yahoo Finance reported similar figures (84% and 15%).

drivers.title: October inflation runs hotter than forecast
drivers.text: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected, and core prices (no food or energy) rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, matching September's pace. Higher-than-expected inflation makes investors demand higher yields on bonds and makes more Fed hikes likely, so the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to about 4.93% this morning from about 4.88% Monday. Lenders typically pass that kind of move along in the same day's rate sheets.

drivers.title: Fed's Waller opens the door to a half-point hike
drivers.text: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said this morning he leans toward a December rate hike and that a larger half-point move should be considered if core inflation came in around 0.3% or higher, which it did. Traders now treat a December 9 hike as close to certain and put the chance of a half-point move near 15%, up from about 1%. Expectations of higher short-term rates make it harder for mortgage rates to fall.

drivers.title: Oil drops below $90 as Iran strikes are put on hold
drivers.text: Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel this morning for the first time since August, and is down more than 20% from its late-October high near $118, after President Trump said new strikes on Iran aren't needed for now following appeals from Qatar's prime minister. Cheaper oil lowers fuel and shipping costs and eases inflation worries, which helps bond yields. The U.S. naval blockade and attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz continue, so this support can fade quickly.

drivers.title: Heavy government bond sales this week
drivers.text: The Treasury is selling $125 billion of 3-, 10- and 30-year debt this week. Monday's 3-year sale drew slightly soft pricing, and today's $42 billion 10-year sale comes right after the inflation surprise. If buyers demand higher yields to take on all that supply, mortgage rates feel it, since they track the 10-year.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.23% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 6, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much, and if markets calm down, there is room for mortgage rates to improve even if Treasury yields stay put.

outlook.basis: The odds have tilted slightly toward higher rates. Inflation ran hotter than forecast for a second straight month, a December Fed hike now looks close to certain, and at least one Fed governor is openly discussing a larger half-point move, which pushed the 10-year Treasury yield up this morning. In borrowers' favor: oil has dropped below $90 a barrel on hopes for calmer relations with Iran, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.23% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), which gives lenders some room to absorb bond-market swings. Big swing events: this week's government bond sales, Friday's wholesale inflation report, Iran headlines, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the early-December jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is still near 7.18%, close to its lowest since late September and down from roughly 7.5% in early October, but this morning's hotter inflation report pushed Treasury yields up, so lender pricing may rise today. If you're under contract or close to it, it's worth talking with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates have eased over the past month, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%, and today's inflation surprise and a likely December Fed hike could keep rates from falling much further. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are near their lowest since September, around 7.18%, but this morning's hotter inflation report pushed bond yields up and a December Fed hike now looks nearly certain.
